tagline: The story of Israel and Judah from Elijah's departure to the fall of Samaria and of Jerusalem, told as the long working out of God's word through prophets and kings.
overview:
Second Kings picks up where 1 Kings stops, with Ahab dead and his son Ahaziah on Israel's throne. Its first half belongs largely to the prophet Elisha, who receives Elijah's mantle when Elijah is taken up in a whirlwind and then works a long series of wonders: purifying a spring, multiplying a widow's oil, raising a Shunammite woman's son, healing the Aramean general Naaman of skin disease, and blinding an Aramean raiding party. Around those stories the politics of the ninth century BC grind on. Moab rebels, Aram besieges Samaria, and then Jehu, anointed at Elisha's command, wipes out the house of Ahab and Jezebel in a bloody coup. In Judah, Ahab's daughter Athaliah seizes power and nearly destroys the line of David, until the priest Jehoiada crowns the hidden boy Joash.

The second half moves faster and darker. Assyria rises in the east and swallows the northern kingdom, and Samaria falls in 722 BC; chapter 17 pauses to explain why, in one of the Bible's longest theological reflections on history. Judah survives for another century and a quarter under a mix of kings. Hezekiah trusts the LORD when the Assyrian king Sennacherib surrounds Jerusalem, and the city is spared. His son Manasseh then leads Judah into the worst idolatry in its history. Josiah finds the Book of the Law in the temple and carries out the most thorough reform any king attempted, but it cannot turn back the judgment. Babylon replaces Assyria, Jerusalem is captured in 597 BC and destroyed in 587 or 586 BC, and the temple burns.

The book ends in exile with a quiet scene: King Jehoiachin, David's descendant, released from a Babylonian prison and given a seat at the king's table. Second Kings matters because it tells, without flinching, how the people of God lost everything they had been given, and it insists that this happened neither by accident nor because other gods were stronger. It also refuses to end in despair. The word of the LORD has proved true in judgment, and the promise to David is still alive.
author:
Like 1 Kings, the book is anonymous, and 1 and 2 Kings were originally a single work. A Jewish tradition preserved in the Babylonian Talmud names the prophet Jeremiah as the author of Kings. The link is real in one respect: 2 Kings 24:18-25:30 appears almost word for word as Jeremiah 52, and the two books share much of their language and outlook. Most scholars today think of an editor or school of editors who shaped older sources into the present book. Those sources are named in the text: the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel and the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah, cited at the end of reign after reign, probably royal annals or works drawn from them. The long Elijah and Elisha narratives likely came from circles of prophets who kept those stories.

Since Martin Noth's work in the 1940s, many scholars have read Deuteronomy through 2 Kings as one Deuteronomistic History, judged by the standards of Deuteronomy: worship of the LORD alone, at the one place he chose. A common view (associated with Frank Moore Cross) sees a first edition in the reign of Josiah, whose reform is the book's high point, and a second edition during the exile that added the fall of Judah. Others argue for one exilic author working with sources. Conservative scholars generally accept the use of sources and editorial shaping while stressing the antiquity and reliability of the material.
date: The book in its final form cannot be earlier than about 561 BC, the year in which the Babylonian king Evil-merodach (Amel-Marduk in Babylonian records) released Jehoiachin from prison, the event told in the last paragraph (2 Kings 25:27-30). It says nothing of Cyrus's decree of 539/538 BC or of any return from exile, so most scholars place its completion in the middle of the sixth century BC, during the exile. Those who hold to an earlier edition under Josiah date it to the late seventh century BC, with the last chapters added later. The events the book covers run from about 852 BC, the death of Ahaziah of Israel, to 561 BC, a span of roughly three centuries. The chronology of the kings is complicated by co-regencies and by different ways of counting the first year of a reign, and scholars have proposed several reconstructions; dates for individual reigns in these notes are therefore approximate.
setting:
Second Kings is the story of a small people caught between empires. In the ninth century BC, Israel's main rival was Aram, the kingdom of Damascus, under kings such as Ben-hadad and Hazael. Assyria, centered on the Tigris in northern Mesopotamia, was already pressing west: Shalmaneser III fought a coalition that included Ahab at Qarqar in 853 BC, and his Black Obelisk shows Jehu, or his envoy, bowing and bringing tribute. From the reign of Tiglath-pileser III (745 to 727 BC), called Pul in 2 Kings 15:19, Assyria turned raiding into conquest, deporting populations and reducing kingdoms to provinces. Samaria fell in 722 BC after a siege begun by Shalmaneser V; his successor Sargon II claimed the capture and the deportation of its people. In 701 BC Sennacherib invaded Judah and besieged Lachish, a campaign known both from his own annals and from the reliefs of Lachish's fall that decorated his palace at Nineveh.

Assyria collapsed at the end of the seventh century. Nineveh fell in 612 BC, Josiah died at Megiddo in 609 BC when he confronted Pharaoh Neco of Egypt, and Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC. The Babylonian Chronicle records Nebuchadnezzar's capture of Jerusalem in 597 BC, and ration tablets from Babylon mention Jehoiachin, king of Judah, receiving provisions in exile. Several discoveries touch the book's world directly: the Mesha Stele, Moab's own account of throwing off Israel's rule (compare 2 Kings 3); the Tel Dan Stele, an Aramaic inscription that refers to the house of David; and the Siloam tunnel inscription, cut into the water tunnel usually connected with Hezekiah (2 Kings 20:20). The first readers were Judeans in Babylon or in the ruins of Judah, asking what their history meant.
purpose: Second Kings was written to explain the catastrophe of exile and to call its readers back to God. Its answer to the question of why the kingdoms fell is stated most fully in 2 Kings 17: Israel and Judah worshiped other gods, ignored the covenant, and refused the prophets the LORD sent to warn them. The fall was judgment, not the defeat of the LORD by the gods of Assyria or Babylon. The book also teaches its readers how to live in the ruins. It shows that repentance matters, even late (Hezekiah and Josiah are honored for it), and that God is patient far longer than anyone deserves. Finally, it keeps hope open. The release of Jehoiachin in the last verses is small, but it tells exiles that David's line has not been extinguished and that the story is not over.
story: Second Kings completes the history that begins in Joshua and runs through Judges, Samuel, and 1 Kings: the people brought into the land lose it. It follows directly from 1 Kings 22, where Ahab dies at Ramoth-gilead as Micaiah foretold. The prophets whose books stand later in the Bible preached during these same reigns: Amos and Hosea to the northern kingdom in the eighth century, Isaiah and Micah in Judah under Hezekiah and his predecessors, and Jeremiah, Zephaniah, and Habakkuk in Judah's last decades. First and 2 Chronicles retell the same period from Judah's side for the community after the exile, and Ezra, Nehemiah, Haggai, and Zechariah tell of the return that 2 Kings does not reach. Lamentations mourns the fall that 2 Kings reports.
christ: Second Kings shows a people who cannot keep covenant and kings who cannot save them, and it ends with the son of David in chains, released into a foreign king's hospitality. The New Testament presents Jesus as the son of David in whom the promise that seemed nearly dead is finally kept, and Jehoiachin (called Jechoniah) stands in the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew 1:11-12. The Elisha stories are especially important for the Gospels. Jesus himself cites Naaman the Syrian, healed when many in Israel were not, as a sign that God's mercy reaches outsiders (Luke 4:27). His feeding of the crowds, with bread left over, echoes Elisha's feeding of a hundred men with twenty loaves (2 Kings 4:42-44), and his raising of the widow's son at Nain, a village near Shunem, recalls Elisha's raising of the Shunammite's son. John the Baptist, dressed like Elijah (2 Kings 1:8; Matthew 3:4), comes in Elijah's role, and Jesus, like Elisha after Elijah, carries on a work of mercy greater than his forerunner's. These are patterns and echoes that the New Testament draws out, not predictions, and they show the kind of king and prophet Israel needed.
reading:
Second Kings is theological history in narrative prose. Its reigns are framed by regnal formulas that give the king's accession, age, length of reign, and (for Judah) his mother's name, followed by a verdict on whether he did what was right or evil in the eyes of the LORD. Northern kings are almost always said to walk in the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, meaning the golden calves at Bethel and Dan. The story alternates between the two kingdoms until Israel falls, so a reader should keep track of which king is meant; confusingly, both kingdoms had kings named Jehoram (or Joram), Ahaziah, and Jehoash (or Joash) at about the same time.

Watch for prophecy and fulfillment: the narrator repeatedly notes that events happened according to the word of the LORD. The Elisha chapters are not a detour from the history but its heart, showing that God is at work in ordinary homes, among foreigners, and in a besieged city while kings fail. Some episodes are morally troubling (the bears in chapter 2, Jehu's massacres in chapters 9 and 10), and the book does not always pause to comment; a careful reader notices that later Scripture sometimes does, as when Hosea condemns the bloodshed at Jezreel (Hosea 1:4).

structure.title: Elijah's last acts and Elisha's succession
structure.summary: Elijah announces Ahaziah's death and calls down fire on the king's soldiers, then is taken up in a whirlwind, and Elisha receives his cloak and his spirit.

structure.title: The ministry of Elisha
structure.summary: Elisha's word shapes a war against Moab, provides for a widow, raises a Shunammite's son, heals Naaman, protects Israel from Aram, and announces relief for starving Samaria and Hazael's rise in Damascus.

structure.title: Jehu's purge and Joash's rescue
structure.summary: Jehu destroys the house of Ahab and the worship of Baal in Israel, while in Judah Athaliah seizes the throne and the boy Joash is hidden, crowned, and later repairs the temple.

structure.title: The last years of Israel
structure.summary: Elisha dies, the two kingdoms rise and decline, Assyria advances, and Samaria falls, followed by a long explanation of why the northern kingdom was exiled.

structure.title: Hezekiah and Manasseh
structure.summary: Hezekiah trusts the LORD and Jerusalem survives Sennacherib's siege, but his son Manasseh fills the land with idolatry and innocent blood.

structure.title: Josiah's reform and the fall of Jerusalem
structure.summary: Josiah finds the Book of the Law and purges the land, but after his death Babylon takes Jerusalem, burns the temple, and carries Judah into exile, where Jehoiachin is at last released from prison.

themes.title: The word of the LORD comes true
themes.body: Second Kings is built on prophecy and fulfillment. Elijah's word about Ahaziah, Elisha's about water, food, and war, the old prophecy against Jezebel, the warnings of the prophets against Israel and Judah: each is fulfilled, and the narrator often says so. History in this book is the arena where God's word proves itself, in mercy and in judgment.

themes.title: Idolatry and its cost
themes.body: Every king is measured by worship. The golden calves of Jeroboam, the Baal worship of Ahab's house, the high places, Manasseh's altars, and the sacrifice of children are not side issues but the reason for the exile. The book treats idolatry as covenant betrayal that corrupts a whole society, including its justice and its treatment of the weak.

themes.title: God's mercy beyond the borders
themes.body: In a book of judgment, Elisha's stories show God caring for widows, a barren woman, starving lepers, and even enemies. Naaman, the commander of a hostile army, is healed and confesses that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel. The God who judges his own people is also the God of the nations.

themes.title: The lamp of David
themes.body: Twice the line of David nearly ends, when Athaliah murders the royal family and when Babylon deposes the last kings, and twice it survives, first in a hidden child and then in a released prisoner. The book never forgets God's promise to David, even when David's sons forget God.

themes.title: Reform and its limits
themes.body: Jehoash, Hezekiah, and Josiah all attempt reform, and the book honors them. Yet it also shows that reform led from the top cannot by itself change a people's heart. Josiah's is the most thorough reform in the book, and still the judgment comes, which leaves readers looking for a deeper renewal than any king could bring.

keyChapters.why: Elijah is taken up to heaven in a whirlwind, and Elisha receives his cloak and a double portion of his spirit, marking the succession of prophetic ministry.
Naaman, an Aramean commander, is healed of skin disease by washing in the Jordan and confesses the God of Israel, a story Jesus later cites.
Jehu is anointed king and destroys Joram, Ahaziah, and Jezebel, fulfilling Elijah's word against the house of Ahab.
Athaliah tries to wipe out the royal line of Judah, and the rescue and crowning of the boy Joash keeps David's line alive.
Samaria falls to Assyria, and the narrator explains at length why the northern kingdom went into exile.
Hezekiah spreads Sennacherib's threatening letter before the LORD, Isaiah answers, and Jerusalem is delivered.
The Book of the Law is found in the temple, and Josiah's response begins the greatest reform in Judah's history.
Jerusalem falls, the temple burns, and the people go into exile, yet the book ends with Jehoiachin released and fed at the king's table.
